messages.body_plain:
Hi

This is happening because you are manually adding lines, instead of "mapping a variable to an easthetic", in ggplot2 language. A more standard way in ggplot2 would be to turn your data-frame into long, where a new variable would indicate the type (estimate versus CI), then you would have geom_line(linetype = variable).

Without a reproducible example from your data, look at this artificial example:

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

tidy(lm(freeny), conf.int <http://conf.int>=TRUE) %>%
  mutate(term = 1:n()) %>%
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high) %>%
  gather(variable, value, -term) %>%
  mutate(type = if_else(str_detect(variable, "estimate"), "estimate", "CI") %>% factor(levels = c("estimate", "CI"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=term, y=value, group=variable, linetype=type))+
  geom_line()

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diana,
Good question. This is a common one, and as always there are a few approaches. As Matthieu showed, you can make your data "long" and more easily assign a variable to a given aesthetic (i.e., linetype, color, fill, etc).

Alternatively, you can use a scale_.._manual option, and assign something specifically to each geom you are interested in using. I've created a fake dataset so you can run this code, in the future, try to attach the data as a txt file or csv if you want folks to try and recreate your specific plot. Or simulate some data (see below for an example). Hope this helps!

Adios,
Ryan

# Load required libraries
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

# Make Some Data
dsr <-  exp(seq(0.98, 0.4, length.out = 25))
Day <- seq(1:25)
lower <-  exp(seq(0.975, 0.38, length.out = 25))
upper <-  exp(seq(0.985, 0.42, length.out = 25))
df <- tibble(Day, dsr, upper, lower)

# Make a plot and assign specific items for the legend inside the aes(), you can rename as you like
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data=df, aes(x=Day, y=dsr, linetype="Estimate"), size = 1.25) +
  geom_line(data=df, aes(x=Day, y=lower, linetype = "CI"), size = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data=df, aes(x=Day, y=upper, linetype = "CI"), size = 0.8) +

  labs(x ="Age of Nest (days)", y ="Cumulative Survival Probability (25-d)") +

  scale_linetype_manual(name="", values=c("Estimate"=1, "CI"=3))+

  ggtitle("Daily Survival Rate", subtitle = "97.24%") +
  theme_classic()+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5, size=16),
        plot.subtitle =element_text(hjust=0.5, size=13),
        axis.line = element_line(size = 1),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 14),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size=15),
        axis.text.x = element_text(face="bold", color="black", size=11),
        axis.text.y = element_text(face="bold", color="black", size=11),
        axis.ticks = element_line(size=1))+

# changed scales slightly to match data
  scale_y_continuous(limits=c(1.2, 3.0), breaks = seq(1.2, 3.0, by =0.2), expand = c(0,0))+
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,25),expand = c(0,0))

messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering about a small nitpicky code thing. When using apply, I often find myself putting 'function(x)' before a prebaked function so that I can refer to portions of the vector that apply is chunking.

For example:

dummy_matrix <- matrix(c(1,2,3,  4,5,6, nrow = 3, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(c(), c("inventive", "column_names")))
apply(dummy_matrix, 1, function(x) some_fancy_function(parameter1 = x["inventive"], parameter2 = x["column_names"])

Specifically, I am trying to figure out if there is another way to point the function to a named portion of the vector other than x["inventive"] or x["column_names"] so that I can code my apply functions like this:

apply(dummy_matrix, 1, some_fancy_function, parameter1 = insertmagicsolutionhere!, parameter2 = insertmagicsolutionhere!)

Thanks!

Hi David,

dummy_matrix <- matrix(c(1,2,3,4,5,6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(c(), c("inventive", "column_names")))

apply(dummy_matrix, 1, sum) # calculate sums over the rows of the matrix
apply(dummy_matrix, 2, sum) # calculate sums over the columns of the matrix

dummy_matrix2 <- matrix(c(1,NA,2,3,4,5,NA,6), nrow = 4, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(c(), c("inventive", "column_names")))

apply(dummy_matrix2, 1, sum) # calculating sums without specifying the "na.rm" argument will fail on some rows
apply(dummy_matrix2, 2, sum) # calculating sums without specifying the "na.rm" argument will fail on both columns

apply(dummy_matrix2, 1, sum, na.rm = TRUE) # no failures with "na.rm" specified
apply(dummy_matrix2, 2, sum, na.rm = TRUE) # no failures with "na.rm" specified

Best,
Evan

messages.body_plain:
Hi David

Let me offer a different way to look at this problem.
For a vectorized some_fancy_function,  you can pass the entire first column and the entire second column of the matrix as 2 separate arguments, e.g.
   some_fancy_function( dummy_matrix[, "inventive"], dummy_matrix[, "column_names"])

This skips the apply() call all together, and uses the vectorized nature of the language, making the code shorter and  arguably "simpler".

This works because some_fancy_function() is vectorized because paste() is. Indeed we could use
    paste( dummy_matrix[, "inventive"], "is", dummy_matrix[, "column_names"], sep = " ")
directly.'

If some_fancy_function() was not vectorized but needed to be called separately for each pair of values in each row of the matrix, you could use

mapply(some_fancy_function,  dummy_matrix[, "inventive"], dummy_matrix[, "column_names"])

So this is an answer to a different but very related question.   Hopefully it steers you towards a different approach to the broader question you're addressing.

You really don't want your function to look back at the input data. In spite of how ostensibly convenient Non-standard Evaluation (NSE) is
for some things, when it bites you, it bites bad.  And you want functions to behave in predictable, reproducible ways when called from different contexts.

D.

messages.subject_clean: D-RUG Listserv: Guidance for best practices
messages.body_plain:
Hi Folks,

Since a new quarter is upon us, we wanted to send something out about our listserv. The Davis R-Users Group (D-RUG) listserv is an awesome environment to pose and answer questions that generally relate to "R" things. We currently have over a 1,000 members on the listserv, and more join each year. So, we (the D-RUG coordinators and community) want to send a friendly reminder on best practices for using this listserv. We'll send this email out once or twice a year, just to refresh everyone, and bring new folks up to speed.

R You Stuck with a Question?

We all get stuck. No matter what your experience/background is, from beginner to expert. So when you get stuck, there are a few options. Before immediately turning to the listserv, try a few of these other options if you can. Sometimes this due diligence will answer your question. Sometimes it won't.

Here are a few options that can help:
You can google a term or problem and see if you can solve your problem, preface your search with [R] to narrow the search.
Great option, used all the time, but hard if you don't know right terms/questions to google
You can see if there's anything useful in the HELP section of RStudio/R (depends on the package and the function...some are well documented others are not)
Try typing "?" + whatever term or function you are trying to use in the console, like: ?mean
Use 2 question marks to look for any function that has the term "mean" in it: ??mean
You can turn to the D-RUG listserv or workgroup meetings!

Help Us Help You (REPRoducible EXamples)

Learning R (or any coding language) can sometimes just be about persistence, due diligence, and repetition. What we as a community want to strive for is making our listserv and work sessions accessible to everyone, and make sure everyone has the opportunity to ask and answer questions. As part of this, if folks asking questions can spend a little extra time trying to build a reproducible example (REPREX), it helps because:
More folks are willing to respond to the question because the questioner has spent time making it easier to answer
Questions with REPREX often get a quicker answer because lots of folks can try out the code and find a solution (or multiple solutions), vs. just a few who may be familiar with the specifics
Everyone learns...because everyone can run the code and see the problem/solution. This is one of the awesome things about the listserv, it's a great place to learn new approaches/tricks!
In making a REPREX, sometimes we answer our own question. It's the "rubber ducky <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber_duck_debugging>" approach
In worksessions, it can mean more time spent helping other folks

Making a REPREX

So how the heck do we make a REPREX <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_working_example>?!? It's a minimum working example, and generally it's helpful to have the following:
required packages/libraries
data (can use a small example dataset or just a snippet of your own data)
minimal and clearly commented code (what is each line doing? where does it break or have a problem?)

Here are some links to tutorials/options which provide more information:
http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Reproducibility.html
https://www.njtierney.com/post/2017/01/11/magic-reprex/
https://community.rstudio.com/t/faq-whats-a-reproducible-example-reprex-and-how-do-i-do-one/5219
https://www.jessemaegan.com/post/so-you-ve-been-asked-to-make-a-reprex/
https://yihui.name/en/2017/09/the-minimal-reprex-paradox/
https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example
https://reprex.tidyverse.org/

R.E.S.P.E.C.T. <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respect_(song)#Aretha_Franklin_version>

Ultimately we want anyone, of any R level (including just beginning!) to feel comfortable asking questions on the D-RUG listserv. Even if that means there is no REPREX. But we also want to respect the time/energy of the folks who kindly respond to questions. So bear that in mind when you are asking, responding, or commenting on the listserv. As always we abide by our Code of Conduct <https://d-rug.github.io/code-of-conduct.html>, and ask our community to do the same.

Thanks much,

your friendly D-RUG coordinators
--

John Muir (My First Summer in the Sierra, 1911)

messages.subject_clean: Announcing MAD 2.0!
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

We are excited to announce MAD 2.0!

Some things will be the same (the time! and usually the place), but other things will be different. Our first week (Oct 2) will launch with an introduction and how-to, so please come by if you'd like to participate this quarter! We'll send a reminder with more info next week.

Description

Meet and Analyze Data (MAD) is a community focused on tackling biological big data questions ranging from high level concepts (what is metagenome assembly?) to low level coding problems (what does this error message even mean!?) and everything in between. Each week will start with a short lesson to share important tools for project management and data analysis designed to help us level up our skills. Then, participants with expertise in a variety of areas will be available to help with individual research and coding questions. To facilitate this discussion, all questions must be posted on the MAD discourse forum <https://mad.oxli.org/>. Help us help you: please try to post your questions ahead of time, and be kind to our helpers as they try to get to all the questions! To keep things fun for everyone, please check out our Code of Conduct <http://ivory.idyll.org/lab/coc.html>.

Schedule
Date Topic
2-Oct MAD 2.0: how to help us help you
9-Oct What is the shell?
16-Oct Practical software management with conda, Pt 1
23-Oct no MAD

6-Nov Project organization and management

20-Nov Quick sequencing data insights with sourmash
27-Nov Thanksgiving -- no MAD
4-Dec Automation with Snakemake, Pt 1
11-Dec Automation with Snakemake, Pt 2

Best,
Your Friendly Neighborhood DIB Lab
